items.title: Life on Foot
items.content:
It’s been transformative, and I wish I’d done it sooner!

Unlike a city, a village has homes with yards. Unlike a suburb, a village has businesses and parks intermixed with homes. It’s the best of both worlds.

Being able to walk or bike places has trickle-down effects.

  • Instead of driving 20 minutes one-way to get groceries, I can ride my bike there in 5 minutes.
    • Because the grocery store is so close, I don’t need to “stock up.” I go every day and buy less with each trip.
    • Because I’m only buying what I need for that day or the next or so, my meats and produce are much fresher.
    • Because I can ride my bike there, I’m getting more exercise every day and spending less time sitting.
  • Because there are so many shops nearby, its easier to go out and do things.
    • Because it’s easier to access entertainment out of the house, I buy less stuff and spend less time at home.
    • Because I need fewer things at home to keep me from being bored, I can give away a lot possessions.
    • Because I have less stuff, it’s easier to keep my house clean and tidy.

Another trickle-down effect of getting out of the house more is that I have a lot more conversations with strangers.

I’ll see a cute dog on the bike path and start talking to its owner. I’ll compliment someone’s shirt in the market and we’ll strike up a conversation. I’ll say hi in passing or wave at a stranger while riding my bike, and they’ll wave back.

These kinds of random interactions are common place in cities, but virtually nonexistent in most suburbs.

A village makes them far more common, and they nourish my soul! It’s something I wasn’t aware I was missing until we moved down here.

I wasn’t really a fan of urbanism because I hate cities.

But now that I’m aware of the village layout—now that I’m basically living in my own Sesame Street—I’m sold! This is my happy place!

items.title: The Village
items.content:
About 14 years ago, we moved out into the rural suburbs. I loved the quiet, the abundant wildlife, and our proximity to farms.

I didn’t realize just how often doing at all would require a car.

Absolutely was walkable. We lived at the very top of a very high hill, so things weren’t really bikeable either.

Groceries, restaurants, entertainment, friends, the library, and so on… you need to get in a car and drive at least 15 minutes for all of it.

And as a result, we became homebodies, and spent a lot of money buying a lot of stuff to make our home a place we had to leave as little as possible.

In a city, any particular block will include a mix of apartments, businesses, and maybe a park or school or playground. No matter where you live, you can walk or bike to get around and get what you need.

By contrast, suburb zoning laws in North America usually prevent this kind of mixed-use development.

Homes are allowed on one side of town. Businesses are allowed on another. They’re typically pretty far from each other.

This means that unless you’re right on the border of these two zones, you a car to do anything.

  1. Walk and bike places, but live in a noisy, busy, crowded space.
  2. Get quiet and peace, but need a car to get anywhere.

But there’s a third option!

In much of Europe (and small pockets of America), you can find villages.

These are suburban spaces. They’re relatively quiet, and have homes with lawns and lots of wildlife around.

But they’re also walkable and bikeable.

The zoning of these spaces allows for small businesses to coexist alongside homes. More restricted commercial use than a city, but far less so than a typical sprawling suburb.

They often have narrower roads, which slows down car traffic, making them more pedestrian friendly, too.

We recently decided we were done with the sprawl, and moved from a rural suburb in Massachusetts to a small coastal village in Rhode Island.

The change in lifestyle that comes from being in a walkable/bikeable area has been transformative, and I’m going to talk all about it in part two!

items.title: We live in a world where...
items.content:
I saw this on Mastodon today (saved the image, lost the source), and it just brought me joy!

Did you know that we live in a world where octopuses dream, otters have a favorite shell that they carry with them all their lives, cows have best friends, and bees have different “dialects” of dance depending on the region?

Or that cats purr at a frequency that accelerates bone healing, the forest grows flowers first after a fire, and dolphins give each other names and respond to them, and Penguins make proposals by giving each other the most beautiful pebble?

…be on the lookout for wonder.

May your day be filled with wonder!
